content: A unicornuate uterus results from the failure of one of the paired Müllerian ducts to elongate, while the other develops normally. This anomaly accounts for approximately 20% of all Müllerian duct anomalies. The embryological tendency for the unicornuate uterus to predominantly occur on the right side remains unexplained. The rate of spontaneous abortion in individuals with a unicornuate uterus is reported to range between 41% and 62%. Premature birth rates in these cases are reported to range from 10% to 20%. Fetal survival rates vary between 38% and 57%, with pooled data suggesting an average survival rate of approximately 40%. Renal abnormalities are more frequently associated with a unicornuate uterus compared to other types of Müllerian duct anomalies. These renal anomalies are reported in 40% of patients with a unicornuate uterus and are always ipsilateral to the rudimentary uterine horn. Renal agenesis is the most commonly reported renal abnormality, occurring in 67% of cases. Diagnosis Hysterosalpingography (HSG) On HSG, the endometrial cavity of a unicornuate uterus typically appears fusiform in shape, tapering at the apex and draining into a single fallopian tube. The uterus is generally displaced off the midline. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) On MRI, the unicornuate uterus appears curved and elongated, with the external uterine contour resembling a banana shape. The uterine volume is reduced, and the configuration of the uterus is asymmetric. Despite these structural abnormalities, the normal zonal anatomy of the myometrium is preserved.
